claim: Mutant huntingtin (mHtt) aggregates associated with Huntington disease transfer anterogradely from presynaptic to postsynaptic neurons in the adult Drosophila olfactory system.
source: Here, we show that mutant huntingtin (mHtt) aggregates associated with Huntington disease transfer anterogradely from presynaptic to postsynaptic neurons in the adult Drosophila olfactory system.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing mHtt aggregate transfer from ORNs to PNs, supported by confocal microscopy and quantification.

claim: Trans-synaptic transmission of mHtt aggregates is inversely correlated with neuronal activity.
source: Trans-synaptic transmission of mHtt aggregates is inversely correlated with neuronal activity and blocked by inhibiting caspases in presynaptic neurons, implicating synaptic dysfunction and cell death in aggregate spreading.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that blocking neuronal activity with shits1 and TeTxLC enhances aggregate transfer, while thermogenetic activation with dTrpA reduces it (Figure 3).

claim: Trans-synaptic transmission of mHtt aggregates is blocked by inhibiting caspases in presynaptic neurons.
source: Trans-synaptic transmission of mHtt aggregates is inversely correlated with neuronal activity and blocked by inhibiting caspases in presynaptic neurons, implicating synaptic dysfunction and cell death in aggregate spreading.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that co-expression of p35 with Httex1Q91-mCherry in DA1 ORNs inhibited formation of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates in DA1 PNs (Figure 6).

claim: mHtt aggregate transmission across synapses requires the glial scavenger receptor Draper.
source: Remarkably, mHtt aggregate transmission across synapses requires the glial scavenger receptor Draper and involves a transient visit to the glial cytoplasm, indicating that phagocytic glia act as obligatory intermediates in aggregate spreading between synaptically-connected neurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that drpr knockout completely blocked formation of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates in postsynaptic PNs (Figure 5).

claim: mHtt aggregate transmission across synapses involves a transient visit to the glial cytoplasm.
source: Remarkably, mHtt aggregate transmission across synapses requires the glial scavenger receptor Draper and involves a transient visit to the glial cytoplasm, indicating that phagocytic glia act as obligatory intermediates in aggregate spreading between synaptically-connected neurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing triple-labeled mCherry+/3xHA+/YFP+ aggregates, indicating that mHtt aggregates from ORNs transit through glial cytoplasm before reaching PNs (Figure 7).

claim: Phagocytic glia act as obligatory intermediates in aggregate spreading between synaptically-connected neurons.
source: Remarkably, mHtt aggregate transmission across synapses requires the glial scavenger receptor Draper and involves a transient visit to the glial cytoplasm, indicating that phagocytic glia act as obligatory intermediates in aggregate spreading between synaptically-connected neurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that mHtt aggregates require passage through glial cytoplasm to reach postsynaptic neurons, and that Draper is required for this process (Figure 7).

claim: A common molecular feature of many neurodegenerative diseases is the misfolding of certain proteins, driving their accumulation into insoluble, amyloid aggregates.
source: A common molecular feature of many neurodegenerative diseases [e.g., Alzheimer disease (AD), frontotemporal dementias (FTD), Parkinson disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and Huntington disease (HD)] is the misfolding of certain proteins, driving their accumulation into insoluble, amyloid aggregates (Knowles et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Knowles et al., 2014.

claim: Appearance of proteinaceous deposits in patient brains correlates closely with neuronal loss and clinical progression.
source: Appearance of proteinaceous deposits in patient brains correlates closely with neuronal loss and clinical progression, and strategies to lower production or enhance clearance of pathological proteins in the degenerating brain have shown therapeutic promise in animal models and clinical trials (Boland et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019; Tabrizi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boland et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019; Tabrizi et al., 2019.

claim: Proteopathic lesions associated with neurodegeneration appear in highly-reproducible and disease-specific spatiotemporal patterns through the brain.
source: Post-mortem histopathological analyses (Braak and Braak, 1991; Braak et al., 2003; Brettschneider et al., 2013) and in vivo imaging studies (Deng et al., 2004; Poudel et al., 2019) indicate that proteopathic lesions associated with neurodegeneration appear in highly-reproducible and disease-specific spatiotemporal patterns through the brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Braak and Braak, 1991; Braak et al., 2003; Brettschneider et al., 2013; Deng et al., 2004; Poudel et al., 2019.

claim: Proteopathic lesion patterns largely follow neuroanatomical tracts, suggesting a central role for synaptic connectivity in pathological aggregate spreading.
source: Interestingly, these patterns largely follow neuroanatomical tracts (Ahmed et al., 2014; Mezias et al., 2017), suggesting a central role for synaptic connectivity in pathological aggregate spreading.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2014; Mezias et al., 2017, and represents an inference from the observed patterns.

claim: Intracellular aggregates formed by tau, α-synuclein, TDP-43, SOD1, and mutant huntingtin transfer from cell to cell and self-replicate by recruiting natively-folded versions of the same protein.
source: Accumulating evidence supports the idea that intracellular aggregates formed by tau, α-synuclein, TDP-43, SOD1, and mutant huntingtin (mHtt) transfer from cell to cell and self-replicate by recruiting natively-folded versions of the same protein, analogous to how infectious prion protein (PrPSc) templates the conformational change of soluble PrPC in prion diseases (Vaquer-Alicea and Diamond, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vaquer-Alicea and Diamond, 2019.

claim: Endocytosis and exocytosis play roles in entry and/or exit of pathogenic protein assemblies from cells.
source: Numerous studies have pointed to roles for endocytosis and exocytosis (Asai et al., 2015; Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015; Chen et al., 2019; Holmes et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010; Zeineddine et al., 2015), membrane permeabilization (Chen et al., 2019; Falcon et al., 2018; Flavin et al., 2017; Zeineddine et al., 2015), tunneling nanotubes (Costanzo et al., 2013; Sharma and Subramaniam, 2019), and neuronal activity (Wu et al., 2016) in entry and/or exit of pathogenic protein assemblies from cells
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Asai et al., 2015; Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015; Chen et al., 2019; Holmes et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010; Zeineddine et al., 2015.

claim: Membrane permeabilization plays a role in entry and/or exit of pathogenic protein assemblies from cells.
source: Numerous studies have pointed to roles for endocytosis and exocytosis (Asai et al., 2015; Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015; Chen et al., 2019; Holmes et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010; Zeineddine et al., 2015), membrane permeabilization (Chen et al., 2019; Falcon et al., 2018; Flavin et al., 2017; Zeineddine et al., 2015), tunneling nanotubes (Costanzo et al., 2013; Sharma and Subramaniam, 2019), and neuronal activity (Wu et al., 2016) in entry and/or exit of pathogenic protein assemblies from cells
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Chen et al., 2019; Falcon et al., 2018; Flavin et al., 2017; Zeineddine et al., 2015.

claim: Tunneling nanotubes play a role in entry and/or exit of pathogenic protein assemblies from cells.
source: Numerous studies have pointed to roles for endocytosis and exocytosis (Asai et al., 2015; Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015; Chen et al., 2019; Holmes et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010; Zeineddine et al., 2015), membrane permeabilization (Chen et al., 2019; Falcon et al., 2018; Flavin et al., 2017; Zeineddine et al., 2015), tunneling nanotubes (Costanzo et al., 2013; Sharma and Subramaniam, 2019), and neuronal activity (Wu et al., 2016) in entry and/or exit of pathogenic protein assemblies from cells
evidence: This claim is supported by citations: Costanzo et al., 2013; Sharma and Subramaniam, 2019.

claim: Neuronal activity plays a role in entry and/or exit of pathogenic protein assemblies from cells.
source: Numerous studies have pointed to roles for endocytosis and exocytosis (Asai et al., 2015; Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015; Chen et al., 2019; Holmes et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010; Zeineddine et al., 2015), membrane permeabilization (Chen et al., 2019; Falcon et al., 2018; Flavin et al., 2017; Zeineddine et al., 2015), tunneling nanotubes (Costanzo et al., 2013; Sharma and Subramaniam, 2019), and neuronal activity (Wu et al., 2016) in entry and/or exit of pathogenic protein assemblies from cells
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2016.

claim: Draper regulates the load of mHtt aggregate pathology in the fly CNS.
source: We and others have previously shown that Draper, a Drosophila scavenger receptor that recognizes and phagocytoses cellular debris (Freeman, 2015), regulates the load of mHtt (Pearce et al., 2015) and Aβ1-42 (Ray et al., 2017) aggregate pathology in the fly CNS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pearce et al., 2015 and Ray et al., 2017.

claim: A portion of phagocytosed neuronal mHtt aggregates gain entry into the glial cytoplasm and nucleate the aggregation of normally-soluble wild-type Htt proteins.
source: Remarkably, we also found that a portion of phagocytosed neuronal mHtt aggregates gain entry into the glial cytoplasm and once there, nucleate the aggregation of normally-soluble wild-type Htt (wtHtt) proteins, suggesting that glial phagocytosis provides a path for spreading of prion-like aggregates in intact brains.
evidence: This claim is based on previous findings by the authors, representing data from prior work.

claim: Microglial ablation suppresses pathological tau transmission between synaptically-connected regions of the mouse brain.
source: Consistent with these findings, microglial ablation suppresses pathological tau transmission between synaptically-connected regions of the mouse brain (Asai et al., 2015), and PrPSc transfers from infected astrocytes to co-cultured neurons (Victoria et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Asai et al., 2015.

claim: PrPSc transfers from infected astrocytes to co-cultured neurons.
source: Consistent with these findings, microglial ablation suppresses pathological tau transmission between synaptically-connected regions of the mouse brain (Asai et al., 2015), and PrPSc transfers from infected astrocytes to co-cultured neurons (Victoria et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Victoria et al., 2016.

claim: HD is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by expansion of a CAG repeat region in exon 1 of the Htt gene.
source: HD is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by expansion of a CAG repeat region in exon 1 of the Htt gene, resulting in production of highly aggregation-prone mHtt proteins containing abnormally expanded polyglutamine (polyQ≥37) tracts (Bates et al., 2015; MacDonald et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bates et al., 2015; MacDonald et al., 1993.

claim: wtHtt proteins containing polyQ≤36 tracts only aggregate upon nucleation by pre-formed Htt aggregate 'seeds'.
source: By contrast, wtHtt proteins containing polyQ≤36 tracts only aggregate upon nucleation by pre-formed Htt aggregate 'seeds' (Chen et al., 2001; Preisinger et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2001; Preisinger et al., 1999.

claim: Pathogenic mHtt aggregates have prion-like properties in cell culture and in vivo models of HD.
source: A growing body of evidence from cell culture (Chen et al., 2001; Costanzo et al., 2013; Holmes et al., 2013; Ren et al., 2009; Sharma and Subramaniam, 2019; Trevino et al., 2012) and in vivo (Ast et al., 2018; Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015; Jeon et al., 2016; Masnata et al., 2019; Pearce et al., 2015; Pecho-Vrieseling et al., 2014) models of HD supports the idea that pathogenic mHtt aggregates have prion-like properties—they transfer from cell to cell and self-replicate by nucleating the aggregation of soluble wtHtt proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations from cell culture and in vivo studies.

claim: mHtt aggregates formed in presynaptic olfactory receptor neuron axons effect prion-like conversion of wtHtt proteins expressed in the cytoplasm of postsynaptic partner projection neurons in the adult fly olfactory system.
source: Here, we report that mHtt aggregates formed in presynaptic olfactory receptor neuron (ORN) axons effect prion-like conversion of wtHtt proteins expressed in the cytoplasm of postsynaptic partner projection neurons (PNs) in the adult fly olfactory system.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Transfer of mHtt aggregates from presynaptic ORNs to postsynaptic PNs was abolished in Draper-deficient animals.
source: Remarkably, transfer of mHtt aggregates from presynaptic ORNs to postsynaptic PNs was abolished in Draper-deficient animals and required passage of the prion-like aggregate seeds through the cytoplasm of phagocytic glial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Transfer of mHtt aggregates from presynaptic ORNs to postsynaptic PNs required passage through the cytoplasm of phagocytic glial cells.
source: Remarkably, transfer of mHtt aggregates from presynaptic ORNs to postsynaptic PNs was abolished in Draper-deficient animals and required passage of the prion-like aggregate seeds through the cytoplasm of phagocytic glial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Aggregates formed by N-terminal fragments of mHtt generated by aberrant splicing or caspase cleavage accumulate in HD patient brains.
source: Aggregates formed by N-terminal fragments of mHtt generated by aberrant splicing (e.g., exon 1; 'Httex1') (Sathasivam et al., 2013) or caspase cleavage (e.g., exon 1–12; 'Httex1-12') (Graham et al., 2006; Figure 1A) accumulate in HD patient brains, are highly cytotoxic, and spread between cells in culture and in vivo (Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015; Costanzo et al., 2013; Pearce et al., 2015; Pecho-Vrieseling et al., 2014; Ren et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sathasivam et al., 2013 and Graham et al., 2006.

claim: N-terminal mHtt fragments are highly cytotoxic.
source: Aggregates formed by N-terminal fragments of mHtt generated by aberrant splicing (e.g., exon 1; 'Httex1') (Sathasivam et al., 2013) or caspase cleavage (e.g., exon 1–12; 'Httex1-12') (Graham et al., 2006; Figure 1A) accumulate in HD patient brains, are highly cytotoxic, and spread between cells in culture and in vivo (Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015; Costanzo et al., 2013; Pearce et al., 2015; Pecho-Vrieseling et al., 2014; Ren et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: N-terminal mHtt fragments spread between cells in culture and in vivo.
source: Aggregates formed by N-terminal fragments of mHtt generated by aberrant splicing (e.g., exon 1; 'Httex1') (Sathasivam et al., 2013) or caspase cleavage (e.g., exon 1–12; 'Httex1-12') (Graham et al., 2006; Figure 1A) accumulate in HD patient brains, are highly cytotoxic, and spread between cells in culture and in vivo (Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015; Costanzo et al., 2013; Pearce et al., 2015; Pecho-Vrieseling et al., 2014; Ren et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015; Costanzo et al., 2013; Pearce et al., 2015; Pecho-Vrieseling et al., 2014; Ren et al., 2009.

claim: wtHttex1 proteins aggregate upon physically encountering mHttex1 aggregate seeds.
source: Our experimental approach (Figure 1B) exploits the previously-reported finding that wtHttex1 proteins aggregate upon physically encountering mHttex1 aggregate seeds (Chen et al., 2001; Preisinger et al., 1999), such that transfer of mHttex1 aggregates from 'donor' cells is reported by conversion of cytoplasmic wtHttex1 from its normally soluble, diffuse state to a punctate, aggregated state in 'acceptor' cells (Figure 1B-inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2001; Preisinger et al., 1999.

claim: In the fly CNS, Httex1Q91 aggregates induce prion-like conversion of normally-soluble Httex1Q25 via a homotypic nucleation reaction that requires the Httex1 sequence.
source: Thus, in the fly CNS, Httex1Q91 aggregates induce prion-like conversion of normally-soluble Httex1Q25 via a homotypic nucleation reaction that requires the Httex1 sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Httex1Q91-mCherry was not detected in DA1 ORNs until ~24 hr before eclosion.
source: We did not detect expression of Httex1Q91-mCherry in DA1 ORNs until ~24 hr before eclosion, consistent with activation of adult olfactory receptor gene expression during late pupal development (Clyne et al., 1999), whereas Httex1Q25-GFP was expressed in PNs via GH146-Gal4 earlier in development (Stocker et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation and citations to Clyne et al., 1999 and Stocker et al., 1997.

claim: Httex1Q91 aggregates first appeared in pharate adults and increased in number as the flies aged.
source: Httex1Q91 aggregates first appeared in pharate adults and increased in number as the flies aged (Figure 1E1'-G1' and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E1'-G1' and J.

claim: Numbers of Httex1Q91 aggregates in males exceeded those in females at each time point.
source: Numbers of Httex1Q91 aggregates in males exceeded those in females at each time point (Figure 1J), consistent with known sexual dimorphism in DA1 glomerular volume (Stockinger et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J and a citation to Stockinger et al., 2005.

claim: Bright Httex1Q25-GFP puncta began to appear and accumulate in the DA1 glomerulus as the flies aged.
source: In these same brains, Httex1Q25-GFP was expressed diffusely throughout GH146+ PN cell bodies and processes in young adults (Figure 1D and E2), but bright Httex1Q25-GFP puncta began to appear and accumulate in the DA1 glomerulus as the flies aged (Figure 1F2 and G2, arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, E2, F2, and G2.

claim: Numbers of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates increased as flies expressing Httex1Q91-mCherry in DA1 ORNs and Httex1Q25-GFP in GH146+ PNs aged from 1 to 21 days old.
source: Numbers of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates increased as flies expressing Httex1Q91-mCherry in DA1 ORNs and Httex1Q25-GFP in GH146+ PNs aged from 1 to 21 days old (Figure 1E2'-G2' and 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E2'-G2' and 1J.

claim: Httex1Q91 aggregates outnumbered Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates at each time point tested.
source: Httex1Q91 aggregates outnumbered Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates at each time point tested (Figure 1J and K), likely reflecting a higher rate of aggregate formation in 'donor' ORNs expressing polyQ-expanded mHttex1 than in 'acceptor' PNs, where wtHttex1 proteins must be nucleated by mHttex1 seeds originating in other cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J and K, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Soluble Httex1Q25-mCherry expressed in DA1 ORNs did not colocalize with Httex1Q25-GFP expressed in PNs.
source: In control experiments, soluble Httex1Q25-mCherry expressed in DA1 ORNs did not colocalize with Httex1Q25-GFP expressed in PNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,E and F), and Httex1Q91 aggregates in DA1 ORNs did not nucleate membrane-bound mCD8-GFP in PNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,E and F.

claim: Httex1Q91 aggregates in DA1 ORNs did not nucleate membrane-bound mCD8-GFP in PNs.
source: In control experiments, soluble Httex1Q25-mCherry expressed in DA1 ORNs did not colocalize with Httex1Q25-GFP expressed in PNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,E and F), and Httex1Q91 aggregates in DA1 ORNs did not nucleate membrane-bound mCD8-GFP in PNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,E and F.

claim: Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates still formed when the Gal4 inhibitor Gal80 was expressed in ORNs.
source: Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates still formed when the Gal4 inhibitor Gal80 was expressed in ORNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,E and F) or when the QF repressor QS was expressed in PNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–F), arguing strongly against co-expression of Httex1Q91-mCherry and Httex1Q25-GFP using the highly-specific Or67d-QF and GH146-Gal4 drivers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,E and F.

claim: Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates still formed when the QF repressor QS was expressed in PNs.
source: Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates still formed when the Gal4 inhibitor Gal80 was expressed in ORNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,E and F) or when the QF repressor QS was expressed in PNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–F), arguing strongly against co-expression of Httex1Q91-mCherry and Httex1Q25-GFP using the highly-specific Or67d-QF and GH146-Gal4 drivers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–F.

claim: mHttex1 aggregates formed in presynaptic ORNs induce non-cell autonomous, homotypic aggregation of wtHttex1 expressed in the cytoplasm of postsynaptic PNs.
source: Together, these findings indicate that mHttex1 aggregates formed in presynaptic ORNs induce non-cell autonomous, homotypic aggregation of wtHttex1 expressed in the cytoplasm of postsynaptic PNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and related supplementary figures.

claim: Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates were not detected in non-synaptically-connected GH146+ PNs.
source: Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates were not detected in non-synaptically-connected GH146+ PNs, including in glomeruli directly adjacent to where DA1 ORNs terminate, suggesting that prion-like conversion of Httex1Q25 in PNs by Httex1Q91 aggregates in ORNs requires synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation and inference.

claim: Prion-like conversion of Httex1Q25 in PNs by Httex1Q91 aggregates in ORNs requires synaptic connectivity.
source: Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates were not detected in non-synaptically-connected GH146+ PNs, including in glomeruli directly adjacent to where DA1 ORNs terminate, suggesting that prion-like conversion of Httex1Q25 in PNs by Httex1Q91 aggregates in ORNs requires synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that aggregates were not detected in non-synaptically-connected PNs.

claim: Httex1Q91 aggregate spreading across ORN-PN synapses is restricted to or much more efficient in the anterograde direction.
source: While many Httex1Q91 aggregates were visible in PN soma, dendrites, and axons in adult brains (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C), we did not observe colocalization of Httex1Q25-GFP and Httex1Q91-mCherry puncta within the antennal lobe neuropil in 1, 7, and 14 day-old adults (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B and D), suggesting that Httex1Q91 aggregate spreading across ORN-PN synapses is restricted to or much more efficient in the anterograde direction.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Aggregates formed by mHttex1-12 caspase-6 cleavage products transfer anterogradely across DA1 ORN-PN synapses.
source: We also found that aggregates formed by mHttex1-12 caspase-6 cleavage products (RFP-Httex1-12Q138) (Figure 1A; Graham et al., 2006), which have previously been shown to spread from ORN axons to more distant (non-PN) neurons in the fly CNS (Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015), also transfer anterogradely across DA1 ORN-PN synapses (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and I, and citations to Graham et al., 2006 and Babcock and Ganetzky, 2015.

claim: Multiple pathogenic N-terminal mHtt fragments share the ability to spread trans-synaptically in Drosophila brains.
source: Together, these findings indicate that multiple pathogenic N-terminal mHtt fragments share the ability to spread trans-synaptically in Drosophila brains, and the sequences required for prion-like conversion of wtHtt reside within Httex1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that both Httex1Q91 and Httex1-12Q138 transfer across synapses.

claim: The sequences required for prion-like conversion of wtHtt reside within Httex1.
source: Together, these findings indicate that multiple pathogenic N-terminal mHtt fragments share the ability to spread trans-synaptically in Drosophila brains, and the sequences required for prion-like conversion of wtHtt reside within Httex1.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that both Httex1Q91 and Httex1-12Q138 can seed wtHttex1 aggregation.

claim: Most (>85%) Httex1Q25-GFP puncta in DA1 PNs colocalized with Httex1Q91-mCherry aggregates.
source: Higher magnification examination of DA1 glomeruli in flies expressing Httex1Q91-mCherry (Figure 2A and B) or RFP-Httex1-12Q138 (Figure 2C and D) in DA1 ORNs and Httex1Q25-GFP in GH146+ PNs revealed that most (>85%) Httex1Q25-GFP puncta in DA1 PNs colocalized with Httex1Q91-mCherry aggregates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: GFP+ surfaces entirely surrounded associated mCherry+ or RFP+ surfaces in colocalized aggregates.
source: Segmentation in both the red (Figure 2A1'-D1') and green (Figure 2A2'-D2') channels demonstrated that GFP+ surfaces entirely surrounded associated mCherry+ or RFP+ surfaces in these colocalized aggregates (Figure 2A3'-D3').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Aggregated Httex1Q91 or Httex1-12Q138 proteins form the 'core' of induced Httex1Q25 aggregates.
source: These data suggest that aggregated Httex1Q91 or Httex1-12Q138 proteins form the 'core' of induced Httex1Q25 aggregates and supports our hypothesis that wtHttex1 solubility in PNs is altered upon direct physical interaction with pre-formed mHtt seeds.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that GFP+ surfaces surround mCherry+ or RFP+ surfaces.

claim: wtHttex1 solubility in PNs is altered upon direct physical interaction with pre-formed mHtt seeds.
source: These data suggest that aggregated Httex1Q91 or Httex1-12Q138 proteins form the 'core' of induced Httex1Q25 aggregates and supports our hypothesis that wtHttex1 solubility in PNs is altered upon direct physical interaction with pre-formed mHtt seeds.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis supported by the experimental data.

claim: Positive FRET signal was detected for all Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates analyzed.
source: Remarkably, positive FRET signal was detected for all Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates analyzed by this method (Figure 2E), indicating that the FP tags fused to each of these proteins were in close molecular proximity (<10 nm apart), consistent with direct physical contact.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The FP tags fused to Httex1Q91 and Httex1Q25 proteins in colocalized aggregates were in close molecular proximity (<10 nm apart).
source: Remarkably, positive FRET signal was detected for all Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates analyzed by this method (Figure 2E), indicating that the FP tags fused to each of these proteins were in close molecular proximity (<10 nm apart), consistent with direct physical contact.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on FRET data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Httex1Q91 and Httex1-12Q138 aggregates increased in size as the flies aged, most substantially during the first week of adulthood.
source: Comparison of volumes for all segmented Httex1Q91, Httex1-12Q138, Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25, and Httex1-12Q138+Httex1Q25 aggregates revealed that Httex1Q91 and Httex1-12Q138 aggregates increased in size as the flies aged, most substantially during the first week of adulthood (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The mean volume of Httex1Q91 or Httex1-12Q138 surfaces that colocalized with Httex1Q25 aggregates was less than the mean volume of all Httex1Q91 or Httex1-12Q138 surfaces.
source: Interestingly, the mean volume of Httex1Q91 or Httex1-12Q138 surfaces that colocalized with Httex1Q25 aggregates (herein referred to as 'seeding-competent' mHtt aggregates) was less than the mean volume of all Httex1Q91 or Httex1-12Q138 surfaces, and these differences were statistically significant in older animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Seeding-competent Httex1Q91 or Httex1-12Q138 aggregates clustered in a subpopulation whose mean was significantly smaller than the mean volume for all Httex1Q91 or Httex1-12Q138 aggregates.
source: When aggregate volumes were analyzed across all time points, it became apparent that seeding-competent Httex1Q91 or Httex1-12Q138 aggregates clustered in a subpopulation whose mean was significantly smaller than the mean volume for all Httex1Q91 or Httex1-12Q138 aggregates (mean Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregate volume = 1.845 ± 0.068 μm3, mean Httex1Q91 aggregate volume = 2.19 ± 0.024 μm3, p=0.0005; mean Httex1-12Q138+Httex1Q25 aggregate volume = 1.293 ± 0.071 μm3, mean Httex1-12Q138 aggregate volume = 2.40 ± 0.048 μm3, p<0.0001) (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Smaller mHttex1 aggregates were associated with increased seeding-propensity and neurotoxicity in other HD models.
source: We previously reported that Httex1Q25 aggregates seeded in the cytoplasm of glial cells colocalized with a similarly smaller-sized subpopulation of seeding-competent Httex1Q91 aggregates from DA1 ORNs (Pearce et al., 2015), and smaller mHttex1 aggregates were associated with increased seeding-propensity and neurotoxicity in other HD models (Ast et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pearce et al., 2015; Ast et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2001.

claim: mHttex1 or mHttex1-12 aggregates formed in presynaptic ORNs effect prion-like conversion of wtHttex1 in the cytoplasm of postsynaptic PNs.
source: Taken together, these findings strongly suggest that mHttex1 or mHttex1-12 aggregates formed in presynaptic ORNs effect prion-like conversion of wtHttex1 in the cytoplasm of postsynaptic PNs, and that mHtt aggregate transmissibility in the fly CNS is correlated with smaller aggregate size.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: mHtt aggregate transmissibility in the fly CNS is correlated with smaller aggregate size.
source: Taken together, these findings strongly suggest that mHttex1 or mHttex1-12 aggregates formed in presynaptic ORNs effect prion-like conversion of wtHttex1 in the cytoplasm of postsynaptic PNs, and that mHtt aggregate transmissibility in the fly CNS is correlated with smaller aggregate size.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing that seeding-competent aggregates are smaller.

claim: Co-expression of shits1 with Httex1Q91-mCherry in DA1 ORNs strongly enhanced formation of seeded Httex1Q25 aggregates in DA1 PN dendrites compared with control flies expressing LacZ.
source: Co-expression of shits1 with Httex1Q91-mCherry in DA1 ORNs in flies shifted from the permissive temperature (18°C) to the restrictive temperature (31°C) in adulthood had no effect or slightly decreased numbers of Httex1Q91 aggregates in the DA1 glomerulus (Figure 3A–C), but, surprisingly, strongly enhanced formation of seeded Httex1Q25 aggregates in DA1 PN dendrites compared with control flies expressing LacZ (Figure 3A,B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Co-expression of Httex1Q91-mCherry with tetanus toxin light chain strongly increased numbers of seeded Httex1Q25 aggregates in the DA1 glomerulus.
source: Likewise, co-expression of Httex1Q91-mCherry with tetanus toxin light chain (TeTxLC), which inhibits SNARE-mediated fusion of synaptic vesicles with presynaptic membranes (Sweeney et al., 1995), strongly increased numbers of seeded Httex1Q25 aggregates in the DA1 glomerulus (Figure 3E,F and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F and H, and a citation to Sweeney et al., 1995.

claim: dTrpA-mediated activation of Httex1Q91-mCherry-expressing DA1 ORNs decreased formation of seeded Httex1Q25 aggregates in the DA1 glomerulus compared with control flies expressing LacZ.
source: In adult flies shifted from ~21°C to 31°C upon eclosion, dTrpA-mediated activation of Httex1Q91-mCherry-expressing DA1 ORNs slightly increased Httex1Q91 aggregate numbers, but decreased formation of seeded Httex1Q25 aggregates in the DA1 glomerulus compared with control flies expressing LacZ (Figure 3I–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I–L.

claim: Prion-like transmission of Httex1Q91 aggregates from ORNs to PNs is inversely correlated with presynaptic ORN activity.
source: Together, these results indicate that prion-like transmission of Httex1Q91 aggregates from ORNs to PNs is inversely correlated with presynaptic ORN activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Aggregate transfer could be enhanced across dysfunctional synapses.
source: These findings suggest that aggregate transfer could be enhanced across dysfunctional synapses, which are an early pathological finding in HD and other neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data and knowledge about HD pathology.

claim: Fluorescence intensity of and volume occupied by DA1 ORN axons were increased ~2 fold in shits1-expressing flies at the restrictive temperature compared with controls expressing LacZ.
source: Segmentation and 3D reconstruction of mCD8-GFP+ DA1 ORN surfaces revealed that fluorescence intensity of and volume occupied by DA1 ORN axons were increased ~2 fold in shits1-expressing flies at the restrictive temperature compared with controls expressing LacZ (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: shits-mediated silencing of Httex1Q91-mCherry-expressing DA1 ORNs may create additional exit sites for Httex1Q91 aggregates.
source: This effect appeared to be specific since Httex1Q91 aggregate abundance in DA1 ORNs was not increased by shits co-expression (Figure 3C), and may reflect a homeostatic compensatory response to endocytic blockade (Davis, 2013; Dickman et al., 2006) that could create additional exit sites for Httex1Q91 aggregates.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on experimental observations and citations to Davis, 2013; Dickman et al., 2006.

claim: Blocking Shibire-mediated endocytosis in DA1 ORNs increased seeded Httex1Q25 aggregate formation in glia without affecting Httex1Q91 aggregate numbers.
source: Similar to effects of shits1 on trans-synaptic Httex1Q91 aggregate transfer, blocking Shibire-mediated endocytosis in DA1 ORNs increased seeded Httex1Q25 aggregate formation in glia without affecting Httex1Q91 aggregate numbers (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D–G.

claim: shits1-mediated silencing of Httex1Q91-mCherry-expressing DA1 ORNs alters axonal surface area and enhances prion-like transfer of Httex1Q91 aggregates from presynaptic ORN axons to the cytoplasm of both glia and postsynaptic PNs.
source: Together, these findings suggest that shits-mediated silencing of Httex1Q91-mCherry-expressing DA1 ORNs alters axonal surface area and enhances prion-like transfer of Httex1Q91 aggregates from presynaptic ORN axons to the cytoplasm of both glia and postsynaptic PNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: drpr knockout completely blocked formation of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates in postsynaptic PNs.
source: Strikingly though, drpr KO completely blocked formation of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates in postsynaptic PNs (Figure 5A,B and D), suggesting that Draper mediates trans-synaptic transfer of mHttex1 aggregates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B and D.

claim: Draper mediates trans-synaptic transfer of mHttex1 aggregates.
source: Strikingly though, drpr KO completely blocked formation of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates in postsynaptic PNs (Figure 5A,B and D), suggesting that Draper mediates trans-synaptic transfer of mHttex1 aggregates.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Enhanced transfer of Httex1Q91 aggregates from shits1-expressing ORNs occurs via the same Draper-dependent mechanism.
source: This surprising effect of drpr KO on seeded Httex1Q25 aggregate formation was also observed when shits1 was co-expressed with Httex1Q91-mCherry in ORNs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), confirming that enhanced transfer of Httex1Q91 aggregates from shits1-expressing ORNs occurs via the same Draper-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: GH146-Gal4 does not drive expression of Httex1Q25-GFP in Draper+ glia.
source: To rule out the possibility that GH146-Gal4 drives expression of Httex1Q25-GFP in Draper+ glia, we used repo-Gal80 to inhibit Gal4 in all glia and saw no effect on Httex1Q91 or Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregate numbers (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B,E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B,E and F.

claim: Expression of drpr-specific siRNAs in PNs did not affect formation of either Httex1Q91 or Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates.
source: Moreover, expression of drpr-specific siRNAs in PNs did not affect formation of either Httex1Q91 or Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F), consistent with glia as the sole source of drpr expression in the fly CNS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F.

claim: Glia are the sole source of drpr expression in the fly CNS.
source: Moreover, expression of drpr-specific siRNAs in PNs did not affect formation of either Httex1Q91 or Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F), consistent with glia as the sole source of drpr expression in the fly CNS.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental data and is consistent with established knowledge.

claim: Neuronal Httex1Q91 aggregates do not seed Httex1Q25 in glial lysosomes or autophagosomes.
source: We also did not observe significant colocalization between ORN-derived Httex1Q91 aggregates and GFP-fusions of Atg8a (Juhász et al., 2008) or Lamp1 (Pulipparacharuvil et al., 2005) in glia (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that neuronal Httex1Q91 aggregates do not seed Httex1Q25 in glial lysosomes or autophagosomes.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3, and citations to Juhász et al., 2008 and Pulipparacharuvil et al., 2005.

claim: Mean volume of Httex1Q91 aggregates in DA1 ORN axons was significantly increased in drpr KO animals compared to wild-type controls.
source: Intriguingly, mean volume of Httex1Q91 aggregates in DA1 ORN axons was significantly increased in drpr KO animals compared to wild-type controls (Figure 5E,F and G-inset), and the relative frequency of two aggregate subpopulations shifted between these genotypes: in the absence of drpr, the abundance of a smaller-sized subpopulation (~0.1–1 μm3) decreased while a larger-sized subpopulation (~2.5–4.0 μm3) increased in abundance (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F and G-inset.

claim: In the absence of drpr, the abundance of a smaller-sized aggregate subpopulation (~0.1–1 μm3) decreased while a larger-sized subpopulation (~2.5–4.0 μm3) increased in abundance.
source: Intriguingly, mean volume of Httex1Q91 aggregates in DA1 ORN axons was significantly increased in drpr KO animals compared to wild-type controls (Figure 5E,F and G-inset), and the relative frequency of two aggregate subpopulations shifted between these genotypes: in the absence of drpr, the abundance of a smaller-sized subpopulation (~0.1–1 μm3) decreased while a larger-sized subpopulation (~2.5–4.0 μm3) increased in abundance (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E–G.

claim: Phagocytic glia could at least in part mediate formation of smaller seeding-competent Httex1 aggregates.
source: Intriguingly, the smaller aggregate subpopulation correlated well with the size of Httex1Q91 aggregates associated with converted Httex1Q25 in PNs (Figure 2G) or glia (Pearce et al., 2015), suggesting that phagocytic glia could at least in part mediate formation of smaller seeding-competent Httex1 aggregates.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on experimental observations and a citation to Pearce et al., 2015.

claim: Molecular features other than size must regulate the seeding capacity of mHttex1 aggregates.
source: However, molecular features other than size must regulate the seeding capacity of mHttex1 aggregates, since smaller-sized aggregates did not completely disappear in drpr KO animals (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Draper-expressing phagocytic glia mediate transfer of Httex1Q91 aggregates across DA1 ORN-PN synapses.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Draper-expressing phagocytic glia mediate transfer of Httex1Q91 aggregates across DA1 ORN-PN synapses, perhaps in part by altering morphological features of neuronal mHttex1 aggregates.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Draper-expressing phagocytic glia may alter morphological features of neuronal mHttex1 aggregates.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Draper-expressing phagocytic glia mediate transfer of Httex1Q91 aggregates across DA1 ORN-PN synapses, perhaps in part by altering morphological features of neuronal mHttex1 aggregates.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on experimental observations.

claim: Dcp-1 cleavage was significantly increased in Httex1Q91- vs Httex1Q25-expressing ORNs when drpr was knocked out.
source: In drprΔ5 heterozygotes, expression of Httex1Q91-GFP in all ORNs did not significantly increase cleavage of Drosophila caspase-1 (Dcp-1) compared to flies expressing Httex1Q25-GFP (Figure 6A,B and E); however, Dcp-1 cleavage was significantly increased in Httex1Q91- vs Httex1Q25-expressing ORNs when drpr was knocked out (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-E.

claim: Glia efficiently clear Httex1Q91-expressing ORN axons displaying Dcp-1-dependent 'eat me' signals via Draper-dependent phagocytosis.
source: These data suggest that glia efficiently clear Httex1Q91-expressing ORN axons displaying Dcp-1-dependent 'eat me' signals via Draper-dependent phagocytosis.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Co-expression of the viral effector caspase inhibitor p35 with Httex1Q91-mCherry in DA1 ORNs inhibited formation of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates in DA1 PNs.
source: In addition, co-expression of the viral effector caspase inhibitor p35 (Hay et al., 1994) with Httex1Q91-mCherry in DA1 ORNs inhibited formation of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates in DA1 PNs (Figure 6F,G,J and K, squares), indicating that inhibition of apoptotic caspases in presynaptic ORNs phenocopies effects of drpr KO on Httex1Q91 aggregate transfer from ORNs to PNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F,G,J and K, and a citation to Hay et al., 1994.

claim: Inhibition of apoptotic caspases in presynaptic ORNs phenocopies effects of drpr KO on Httex1Q91 aggregate transfer from ORNs to PNs.
source: In addition, co-expression of the viral effector caspase inhibitor p35 (Hay et al., 1994) with Httex1Q91-mCherry in DA1 ORNs inhibited formation of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates in DA1 PNs (Figure 6F,G,J and K, squares), indicating that inhibition of apoptotic caspases in presynaptic ORNs phenocopies effects of drpr KO on Httex1Q91 aggregate transfer from ORNs to PNs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Co-expression of p35 with Httex1Q25-GFP in PNs did not affect numbers of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates in the DA1 glomerulus.
source: By contrast, co-expression of p35 with Httex1Q25-GFP in PNs did not affect numbers of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates in the DA1 glomerulus (Figure 6H–K, circles), suggesting that caspase-dependent signaling in PNs is not required for Httex1Q91 aggregate spreading across ORN-PN synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H–K.

claim: Caspase-dependent signaling in PNs is not required for Httex1Q91 aggregate spreading across ORN-PN synapses.
source: By contrast, co-expression of p35 with Httex1Q25-GFP in PNs did not affect numbers of Httex1Q91+Httex1Q25 aggregates in the DA1 glomerulus (Figure 6H–K, circles), suggesting that caspase-dependent signaling in PNs is not required for Httex1Q91 aggregate spreading across ORN-PN synapses.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Signals mediated by apoptotic caspase activation in DA1 ORNs promote engulfment and trans-synaptic transfer of Httex1Q91 aggregates via phagocytic glia.
source: Together, these results suggest that signals mediated by apoptotic caspase activation in DA1 ORNs, and not DA1 PNs, promote engulfment and trans-synaptic transfer of Httex1Q91 aggregates via phagocytic glia.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: mCherry+/3xHA+ puncta representing Httex1Q91 aggregates that transferred from ORNs to glia first appeared in 2 day-old adults and increased in number over the next ~24 hr.
source: mCherry+/3xHA+ puncta representing Httex1Q91 aggregates that transferred from ORNs to glia first appeared in 2 day-old adults and increased in number over the next ~24 hr (Figure 7E,F and J, blue bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E,F and J.

claim: mCherry+/3xHA+/YFP+ puncta began to appear in 2 day-old adults and increased in abundance until the flies were ~4 days old.
source: Remarkably, mCherry+/3xHA+/YFP+ puncta also began to appear in 2 day-old adults and increased in abundance until the flies were ~4 days old (Figure 7F,G and J, striped bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F,G and J.

claim: The timing of appearance of different aggregate subtypes supports the hypothesis that Httex1Q91 seeds originating in DA1 ORN axons transit through the glial cytoplasm before reaching the cytoplasm of DA1 PN dendrites.
source: The timing of appearance of these different aggregate subtypes supports our hypothesis that Httex1Q91 seeds originating in DA1 ORN axons transit through the glial cytoplasm before reaching the cytoplasm of DA1 PN dendrites (Figure 7A, route 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: mCherry+/YFP+ puncta representing aggregates that had transferred from DA1 ORNs to DA1 PNs without accessing the glial cytoplasm were not detected.
source: mCherry+/YFP+ puncta representing aggregates that had transferred from DA1 ORNs to DA1 PNs without accessing the glial cytoplasm were not detected in these brains, arguing against direct transfer of Httex1Q91-mCherry aggregates from ORNs to PNs (Figure 7A, route 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation.

claim: Httex1Q25 aggregates in glia or PNs were only detected when Httex1Q91 was expressed in ORNs.
source: Control animals expressing Httex1Q25 proteins in paired combinations of ORNs, glia, or PNs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) confirmed that Httex1Q25 aggregates in glia or PNs were only detected when Httex1Q91 was expressed in ORNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: When drpr was knocked down in glia using RNAi, numbers of Httex1Q91-mCherry aggregates increased.
source: Remarkably, when we used RNAi to specifically knockdown drpr in glia, numbers of Httex1Q91-mCherry aggregates increased (Figure 7H and I), while mCherry+/3xHA+ and mCherry+/3xHA+/YFP+ aggregates significantly decreased or were absent in 7 day-old adults (Figure 7H and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H and I.

claim: When drpr was knocked down in glia using RNAi, mCherry+/3xHA+ and mCherry+/3xHA+/YFP+ aggregates significantly decreased or were absent in 7 day-old adults.
source: Remarkably, when we used RNAi to specifically knockdown drpr in glia, numbers of Httex1Q91-mCherry aggregates increased (Figure 7H and I), while mCherry+/3xHA+ and mCherry+/3xHA+/YFP+ aggregates significantly decreased or were absent in 7 day-old adults (Figure 7H and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H and J.

claim: Glial Draper mediates Httex1Q91 aggregate transmission from ORN axons to glia and across ORN-PN synapses.
source: These data confirm that glial Draper mediates Httex1Q91 aggregate transmission from ORN axons to glia and across ORN-PN synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Phagocytic glia act as obligatory intermediates in unidirectional prion-like spreading of mHttex1 aggregates from presynaptic ORNs to postsynaptic PNs in Drosophila brains.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that phagocytic glia act as obligatory intermediates in unidirectional prion-like spreading of mHttex1 aggregates from presynaptic ORNs to postsynaptic PNs in Drosophila brains.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: mHttex1 aggregates transfer anterogradely from presynaptic ORNs to postsynaptic PNs via an obligatory path through phagocytic glia in Drosophila brains.
source: In this study, we report that mHttex1 aggregates transfer anterogradely from presynaptic ORNs to postsynaptic PNs via an obligatory path through phagocytic glia in Drosophila brains.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: ORN-to-PN transmission of mHttex1 aggregates was enhanced by blocking endocytosis and exocytosis.
source: ORN-to-PN transmission of mHttex1 aggregates was enhanced by blocking endocytosis and exocytosis and slowed by thermogenetically stimulating presynaptic ORNs, suggesting an inverse relationship between presynaptic activity and mHttex1 aggregate spreading.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ORN-to-PN transmission of mHttex1 aggregates was slowed by thermogenetically stimulating presynaptic ORNs.
source: ORN-to-PN transmission of mHttex1 aggregates was enhanced by blocking endocytosis and exocytosis and slowed by thermogenetically stimulating presynaptic ORNs, suggesting an inverse relationship between presynaptic activity and mHttex1 aggregate spreading.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is an inverse relationship between presynaptic activity and mHttex1 aggregate spreading.
source: ORN-to-PN transmission of mHttex1 aggregates was enhanced by blocking endocytosis and exocytosis and slowed by thermogenetically stimulating presynaptic ORNs, suggesting an inverse relationship between presynaptic activity and mHttex1 aggregate spreading.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: mHttex1 aggregate transfer across synapses was inhibited by blocking apoptosis in presynaptic neurons.
source: mHttex1 aggregate transfer across synapses was inhibited by blocking apoptosis in presynaptic neurons and required the Draper scavenger receptor, which we have previously reported to mediate phagocytic engulfment of mHttex1 aggregates from ORN axons and prion-like conversion of wtHttex1 in the glial cytoplasm (Pearce et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Phagocytosed neuronal mHttex1 aggregates transit through the cytoplasm of glia before reaching postsynaptic PNs.
source: Here, we expand our understanding of the role that glia play in prion-like diseases by showing that phagocytosed neuronal mHttex1 aggregates transit through the cytoplasm of glia before reaching postsynaptic PNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: These findings are the first to uncover a role for a well-conserved phagocytic pathway in prion-like spreading of pathogenic aggregates between neurons in vivo.
source: To the best of our knowledge, these findings are the first to uncover a role for a well-conserved phagocytic pathway in prion-like spreading of pathogenic aggregates between neurons in vivo.
evidence: This claim is an assertion by the authors about the novelty of their findings.

claim: Intrinsic differences in proteostatic capacity of neuronal subpopulations could underlie regional selectivity to inclusion body formation in HD brains.
source: The increased propensity of mHtt to aggregate as a result of polyQ expansion is held in check by the proteostasis network, and intrinsic differences in proteostatic capacity of neuronal subpopulations could underlie regional selectivity to inclusion body formation in HD brains (Margulis and Finkbeiner, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Margulis and Finkbeiner, 2014.

claim: Aggregate spreading could contribute to HD pathogenesis by propagating mHtt pathology through networks of synaptically-connected but selectively-vulnerable neurons.
source: However, accumulating evidence that mHtt aggregates have prion-like properties suggests that aggregate spreading could also contribute to HD pathogenesis by propagating mHtt pathology through networks of synaptically-connected but selectively-vulnerable neurons.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on accumulating evidence.

claim: Some of the earliest changes seen in HD patient brains involve loss of presynaptic cortical inputs to the striatum.
source: Some of the earliest changes seen in HD patient brains involve loss of presynaptic cortical inputs to the striatum, where more prominent pathological findings (e.g., mHtt aggregate accumulation and massive loss of medium spiny neurons) appear in later stages of disease (Reiner and Deng, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reiner and Deng, 2018.

claim: Selective silencing of mHtt in both the cortex and striatum of BACHD mice inhibited striatal degeneration and motor phenotypes to a greater extent that silencing in just the striatum.
source: In addition, selective silencing of mHtt in both the cortex and striatum of BACHD mice inhibited striatal degeneration and motor phenotypes to a greater extent that silencing in just the striatum (Wang et al., 2014), suggesting that mHtt-induced toxicity in presynaptic cortical regions could play an important role in early HD development.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: mHtt-induced toxicity in presynaptic cortical regions could play an important role in early HD development.
source: In addition, selective silencing of mHtt in both the cortex and striatum of BACHD mice inhibited striatal degeneration and motor phenotypes to a greater extent that silencing in just the striatum (Wang et al., 2014), suggesting that mHtt-induced toxicity in presynaptic cortical regions could play an important role in early HD development.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on a citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Presynaptic dysfunction may be a driving force for mHtt aggregate spreading between synaptically-connected regions of the brain.
source: Thus, presynaptic dysfunction may be a driving force for mHtt aggregate spreading between synaptically-connected regions of the brain.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Glial responses to pathological changes in synapses mediate spreading of toxic aggregates between neurons.
source: While our findings do not directly address secondary consequences of mHttex1 aggregate spreading across synapses, we identify a novel mechanism whereby glial responses to pathological changes in synapses mediate spreading of toxic aggregates between neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upon sensing neuronal insult or injury, reactive microglia and astrocytes undergo dramatic morphological, metabolic, and transcriptional changes and promote neuronal survival by releasing trophic factors and phagocytosing debris.
source: Upon sensing neuronal insult or injury, reactive microglia and astrocytes undergo dramatic morphological, metabolic, and transcriptional changes and promote neuronal survival by releasing trophic factors and phagocytosing debris (Hammond et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hammond et al., 2018.

claim: Rare variants in the microglial phagocytic receptor gene TREM2 are associated with increased risk of AD, FTD, and PD.
source: For example, rare variants in the microglial phagocytic receptor gene TREM2 are associated with increased risk of AD, FTD, and PD, and loss of TREM2 function exacerbates Aβ-, tau-, and α-synuclein-associated neurotoxicity (Griciuc et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2019; Leyns et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Griciuc et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2019; Leyns et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2018.

claim: Loss of TREM2 function exacerbates Aβ-, tau-, and α-synuclein-associated neurotoxicity.
source: For example, rare variants in the microglial phagocytic receptor gene TREM2 are associated with increased risk of AD, FTD, and PD, and loss of TREM2 function exacerbates Aβ-, tau-, and α-synuclein-associated neurotoxicity (Griciuc et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2019; Leyns et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Griciuc et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2019; Leyns et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2018.

claim: Disruptions in key glial phagocytic functions leads to accumulation of potentially toxic aggregates in the brain.
source: Disruptions in key glial phagocytic functions leads to accumulation of potentially toxic aggregates in the brain (Asai et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2016; Pearce et al., 2015; Ray et al., 2017; Wilton et al., 2019), and administration of antibodies targeting pathological Aβ, tau, or α-synuclein proteins inhibits aggregate accumulation and spreading in vivo (Funk et al., 2015; Masliah et al., 2005; Tran et al., 2014; Yanamandra et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Asai et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2016; Pearce et al., 2015; Ray et al., 2017; Wilton et al., 2019.

claim: Administration of antibodies targeting pathological Aβ, tau, or α-synuclein proteins inhibits aggregate accumulation and spreading in vivo.
source: Disruptions in key glial phagocytic functions leads to accumulation of potentially toxic aggregates in the brain (Asai et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2016; Pearce et al., 2015; Ray et al., 2017; Wilton et al., 2019), and administration of antibodies targeting pathological Aβ, tau, or α-synuclein proteins inhibits aggregate accumulation and spreading in vivo (Funk et al., 2015; Masliah et al., 2005; Tran et al., 2014; Yanamandra et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Funk et al., 2015; Masliah et al., 2005; Tran et al., 2014; Yanamandra et al., 2013.

claim: Chronically-active or otherwise dysfunctional glia induce neuroinflammation and exacerbate neuronal damage.
source: However, chronically-active or otherwise dysfunctional glia induce neuroinflammation and exacerbate neuronal damage.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Hyperactivate microglia excessively engulf synapses in pre-plaque AD mouse brains.
source: For example, hyperactivate microglia excessively engulf synapses in pre-plaque AD mouse brains (Hong et al., 2016) and signal for formation of neurotoxic A1 astrocytes, which accumulate in several neurodegenerative diseases (Liddelow et al., 2017; Yun et al., 2018) and during aging (Clarke et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hong et al., 2016.

claim: Hyperactivate microglia signal for formation of neurotoxic A1 astrocytes, which accumulate in several neurodegenerative diseases and during aging.
source: For example, hyperactivate microglia excessively engulf synapses in pre-plaque AD mouse brains (Hong et al., 2016) and signal for formation of neurotoxic A1 astrocytes, which accumulate in several neurodegenerative diseases (Liddelow et al., 2017; Yun et al., 2018) and during aging (Clarke et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liddelow et al., 2017; Yun et al., 2018; Clarke et al., 2018.

claim: Rebalancing the protective and harmful effects of glial phagocytosis could be an effective new therapeutic strategy.
source: Our findings thus add new insights to recognizing glia as double-edged players in neurodegeneration and suggest that rebalancing the protective and harmful effects of glial phagocytosis could be an effective new therapeutic strategy.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Glia engulf mHttex1 aggregates, or perhaps portions of mHttex1 aggregate-containing axons, from ORNs without internalizing elements of PNs.
source: We provide several lines of evidence to support a model in which glia engulf mHttex1 aggregates, or perhaps portions of mHttex1 aggregate-containing axons, from ORNs without internalizing elements of PNs: (i) mHttex1 aggregate transmission occurred exclusively in the anterograde direction across ORN-PN synapses, (ii) neuronal mHttex1 aggregates did not colocalize with markers of lysosomes or autophagosomes in glia, and (iii) caspase inhibition in ORNs and not in PNs inhibited aggregate transfer.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Glia selectively target presynaptic ORNs by recognizing apoptotic 'eat me' signals induced by mHttex1 aggregate accumulation.
source: Our data suggest that glia selectively target presynaptic ORNs by recognizing apoptotic 'eat me' signals induced by mHttex1 aggregate accumulation, and this process drives aggregate transfer to postsynaptic PNs.

claim: Aggregate transfer at early ages is restricted to synaptic regions ensheathed by only 1–2 glial cells.

evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental observations and citations to MacDonald et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2017.
